PullRequest.Title: github: avoid throttling generic 403 denials
PullRequest.Body:
Related: microsoft/vscode-internalbacklog#9678

Address GitHub protocol-audit finding: a generic HTTP 403 permission refusal containing "Rate Limit Exceeded" must remain an authorization error, not invent a shared quota cooldown.

- Share one internal HTTP evidence classifier between transport errors, response telemetry and the GitHub cooldown coordinator.
- Retain primary exhaustion from valid remaining-zero headers, HTTP 429, valid Retry-After, or an explicit primary-limit message without usable remaining-quota feedback. Retain explicit secondary-limit headers/messages, reset timing, Retry-After precedence and the existing unhinted cooldown floor.
- Reject malformed numeric and Retry-After evidence on HTTP refusals, and preserve already-established cooldowns when a concurrent response reports healthy quota.
- Keep storage-origin download 403s as authorization failures. Reads/mutations, bootstrap credentials, cancellation/deadlines and account/host isolation keep their existing execution paths.

RegressionFixes.Mechanism: A generic authorization denial was stored as a negative cooldown entry, delaying all later requests for the same account/resource for at least 60 seconds despite healthy quota.
RegressionFixes.Symptom: After a generic 403 containing "Rate Limit Exceeded", otherwise valid REST, GraphQL, download, or bootstrap work for the same quota bucket could remain queued or time out behind an invented 60-second cooldown.
RegressionFixes.FixedBehavior: The shared classifier now accepts a generic 403 body only when exhausted-quota or Retry-After evidence exists, or when the explicit "API rate limit exceeded" message has no usable remaining-quota feedback. Healthy-quota generic denials remain authorization failures and no longer create the 60-second queued-request delay.
RegressionFixes.Evidence: In the base revision, line 107 classified any HTTP 403 body containing "rate limit" as throttling. updateFromResponse then assigned the unhinted 60,000 ms blockedUntil, CooldownState.getDelay exposed that delay, and RequestQueue skipped matching account/resource requests until its wake timer. The added bootstrap test exercises the concrete trigger—a 403 body "Rate Limit Exceeded" with x-ratelimit-remaining: 4999—and verifies that subsequent requests should dispatch without a cooldown.

Scenarios.Scenario: Authenticated REST and GraphQL requests receiving HTTP 403/429 responses
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Queue admission, one network response, bounded body read/decoding, shared quota classification, and error construction are on the request critical path. Classification is synchronous but bounded by the existing maximum response size and replaces repeated lowercase-string checks; it does not add a blocking boundary.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dispatch a GitHub REST or GraphQL HTTP request and read its bounded response body.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One wire call per admitted mutation or unique read, with identical reads coalesced; eligible reads can make one bounded retry only for network/5xx failures, not for 403/429 responses.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same network request and bounded body read occurred. A generic 403 body containing "rate limit" could incorrectly create a 60-second cooldown; this PR removes that delay unless authoritative quota evidence exists.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The response must complete before classification and caller progress; a real cooldown delays later matching account/resource requests in the queue.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Unique requests after read coalescing, partitioned by account and REST resource; response-body classification scales linearly only up to the existing bounded response size.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The existing queue bounds total concurrency to 4, host concurrency to 2, caller concurrency to 2, and admits only one active request per account key. Identical GET/GraphQL reads coalesce before dispatch; the diff does not alter these limits.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: GETs remain coalesced by account, URL, representation, and ETag mode; response classification does not add or bypass representation-cache entries. Cooldown state is keyed by account/resource, and healthy generic denials now avoid the prior false negative-cache entry while established concurrent cooldowns remain preserved.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: transport call flow, cooldown state, queue gating, and focused tests establish both the old false delay and the new evidence requirements.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact prevalence of generic GitHub permission denials using this wording is not measured, but the prior 60-second queue delay and the changed classification path are directly established.
Scenarios.Verdict: No diff-introduced performance regression. The change fixes a concrete false-cooldown latency regression and does not add network calls, retries, fan-out, or unbounded processing.

Scenarios.Scenario: Authenticated API downloads and redirects, including storage-origin 403 denials
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Queue admission and each bounded redirect/network response are critical. An authenticated API 403 reads only the bounded diagnostic prefix before classification; unauthenticated storage failures cancel the body and surface directly.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Fetch the API download URL and follow bounded redirects to content storage.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One initial request plus a bounded sequential request per redirect; the diff adds no request or retry.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same redirect chain and body handling occurred; generic authenticated 403 wording could establish a false cooldown, while the change additionally keeps unauthenticated storage-origin 403s as authorization failures.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Each redirect and final response is on the download critical path. Classification only determines whether future API-origin work is cooled down.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Sequential redirect count up to the existing hard limit and the bounded diagnostic-body byte cap.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Downloads use the same bounded request queue and per-account serialization. Redirect following is sequential and bounded by the existing redirect limit.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Downloads are not representation-cached. Cooldown checks apply only while the request remains authenticated to the API origin; redirected storage-origin denials do not create GitHub account cooldown state.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: authenticated-state transitions and update/classification calls are explicit in the download loop.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Actual redirect depth and denial frequency vary, but both remain bounded and unchanged.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance finding: no new boundary, fan-out, allocation growth, or concurrency change is introduced.

Scenarios.Scenario: Bootstrap credential requests after a generic permission denial or token replacement
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Credential acquisition submits a bootstrap GET through the shared queue. Any account/resource cooldown is on the critical path and can notify or fail callers by deadline; removing the false cooldown allows the next request to dispatch immediately.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Issue authenticated bootstrap GitHub API reads used during credential resolution.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One wire call per unique bootstrap read after coalescing; the added behavior does not retry or duplicate the denied request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same API calls occurred, but generic 403 wording could park both current and subsequent bootstrap work. The new classifier avoids that invented delay while retaining legitimate shared cooldowns.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The request is on credential-resolution critical path; prior false cooldown state could block following or replacement-token reads for 60 seconds.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Unique bootstrap reads and callers sharing the same bootstrap account/origin key after coalescing.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The shared queue limits apply, and identical bootstrap reads coalesce. Credential replacement does not create additional parallel dispatch in the changed code.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Bootstrap GETs retain existing read coalescing. Cooldowns remain shared according to known/unknown bootstrap account keys, but a healthy-quota generic 403 no longer creates a cooldown; legitimate cooldowns still survive client disposal and token replacement.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the bootstrap test covers known and unknown account IDs, immediate follow-up, and replacement credentials.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number of users encountering this exact denial text is unknown; the latency mechanism is deterministic when triggered.
Scenarios.Verdict: Performance-positive regression fix; no new cost is introduced.

Scenarios.Scenario: Concurrent quota observations and successful REST exhaustion
Scenarios.CriticalPath: State updates are synchronous in-memory map writes and event notifications after each response. Matching future requests consult this state during queue selection; no filesystem, IPC, subprocess, database, or additional network operation is added.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Receive concurrent GitHub responses carrying quota headers.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: No extra wire calls; each existing response produces the same bounded number of in-memory state updates as before.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Responses already updated cooldown state. The diff changes evidence validation and preservation semantics without adding boundary calls.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Only legitimately exhausted quota delays later matching requests until Retry-After/reset; unrelated resources/accounts remain available.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Active account/resource keys and existing response count; each update is constant work aside from bounded event listeners and body classification already covered above.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Concurrent HTTP responses may update one account/resource state, but network dispatch remains bounded by the existing queue. Updates are constant-size and use max preservation rather than scheduling parallel work.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cooldown state preserves the maximum active blocked-until value so a later healthy observation cannot erase another in-flight response's established wait. Successful remaining-zero REST responses now retain the authoritative reset as cooldown state; expired entries remain bounded by existing account cleanup.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: coordinator state transitions, account/resource keys, queue delay lookup, and concurrent-response tests directly establish behavior.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Reset durations are server supplied and workload-specific, but state size remains one fixed record per active account/resource and cleanup ownership is unchanged.
Scenarios.Verdict: No actionable regression. Added waits correspond to authoritative exhausted quota and prevent futile boundary traffic; healthy concurrent observations do not shorten an existing cooldown.

Analysis.Summary: Reviewed all six changed files and all diff pages. Traced REST, GraphQL, downloads, bootstrap credentials, telemetry classification, cooldown storage, queue gating, retries, redirects, coalescing, cleanup, and concurrent quota observations. No performance finding was introduced. Recorded the PR as fixing the false 60-second cooldown regression introduced by commit 6a60e32fab82e03830238273f20cef26128602d8.
